content: Nicotine poisoning has historically been associated with its use as an insecticide, though this application is now less common. Each year, numerous children are admitted to emergency rooms after ingesting cigarettes or cigarette butts. A dose of 60 milligrams of nicotine, equivalent to the nicotine content in three packs of cigarettes or half a cigar (if fully absorbed), has the potential to be lethal for an adult. However, regular smokers may have a slightly higher tolerance, though not significantly so. In toddlers, consuming the nicotine content of just one cigarette can result in severe illness. Additionally, cases of nicotine poisoning in children have been reported due to exposure to topical medicinal creams containing nicotine. Individuals involved in the harvesting or cultivation of tobacco may develop Green Tobacco Sickness (GTS), a form of nicotine poisoning caused by dermal absorption of nicotine from wet tobacco leaves. Symptoms of nicotine poisoning include vomiting, nausea, diarrhea, headaches, difficulty breathing, pallor, sweating, palpitations, stomach pain or cramps, seizures, weakness, excessive drooling (or increased drooling in toddlers), and skin lesions. The latter may occur due to prolonged chain-smoking or overuse of nicotine patches or chewing gum. The physiological basis of these symptoms lies in the overstimulation of nicotinic cholinergic neurons. Nicotine initially induces a brief stimulatory phase, followed by a prolonged inhibitory phase that can result in neuromuscular blockade. While some symptoms of nicotine poisoning overlap with those of organophosphate insecticide poisoning, the mechanisms differ. Organophosphates inhibit the enzyme acetylcholinesterase, leading to an accumulation of acetylcholine and overstimulation of all cholinergic neurons, resulting in a broader range of symptoms. In contrast, nicotine specifically targets nicotinic cholinergic receptors, producing a more limited set of symptoms. Diagnosis of nicotine poisoning is confirmed by detecting elevated levels of nicotine or its metabolite, cotinine, in the urine or blood, or by measuring increased serum nicotine concentrations.
